page.mentor_intro: Acute diarrhoea is one of the commonest presentations in any setting — and one where restraint is the evidence-based skill. Most adult infectious diarrhoea, traveller's included, is viral or self-limiting bacterial disease managed with rehydration alone; the art is identifying who needs stool testing, who needs antibiotics, and who needs admission. Inflammatory features (blood, mucus, fever, severe pain) predict bacterial aetiology and shape empiric choices, while the pretravel consultation adds prevention: food and water precautions, and standby antibiotics for high-risk itineraries. Norovirus remains the commonest overall cause — a diagnosis of clinical and infection-control consequence.

teaching_points.claim: Most acute diarrhoea in adults is self-limiting; oral rehydration is the foundation of therapy, with antibiotics reserved for suspected bacterial dysentery, severe disease, or specific risk factors.
Inflammatory features (bloody stool, fever, tenesmus, severe abdominal pain) distinguish dysentery from watery diarrhoea and drive stool-culture and empiric-antibiotic decisions.
Norovirus is the commonest cause of gastroenteritis overall; recognition matters for infection control and because antibiotics have no role.

Traveller's diarrhoea management combines rehydration, loperamide for non-bloody cases, and standby antibiotics (fluoroquinolone or azithromycin) for moderate-to-severe cases on high-risk itineraries.

uncertainties: Whether routine probiotic use shortens acute diarrhoea in adults remains inconsistent across trials.
Optimal empiric antibiotic choice is shifting with fluoroquinolone-resistance patterns in Campylobacter and Shigella.

page.mentor_intro: Where topic 931 covers the general management of diarrhoea, this topic is about the organism-level decision that catches clinicians out: whether to give antibiotics. Campylobacter and non-typhoidal Salmonella mostly need no antibiotics in the well adult; suspected Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli (STEC O157) is the dangerous exception in reverse — antibiotics increase haemolytic uraemic syndrome risk and must be avoided. Norovirus needs neither antibiotics nor testing in most settings, but strict infection control. The single most testable pearl: bloody diarrhoea plus exposure to undercooked beef equals no antibiotics, and HUS surveillance — the syndrome that defines thrombotic microangiopathy in this context.

teaching_points.claim: Antibiotics are indicated for severe suspected bacterial gastroenteritis, dysentery in specific groups, and confirmed treatable pathogens; most Campylobacter and non-typhoidal Salmonella infections in healthy adults resolve without them.

In suspected or confirmed STEC (E. coli O157) infection, antibiotics are contraindicated because they increase the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome; management is supportive with vigilant renal monitoring.

HUS is defined by the triad of non-immune haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury from thrombotic microangiopathy; STEC is the dominant trigger and TTP the key differential within the TMA spectrum.
Norovirus, the commonest gastroenteritis cause, requires no antibiotics and no specific testing in sporadic adult cases; outbreak settings demand environmental disinfection and exclusion policies.

uncertainties: Whether antibiotics benefit bloody Campylobacter dysentery in otherwise healthy adults is debated; practice varies.
Optimal HUS management (hydration strategy, plasma exchange indications versus TTP) follows centre protocols rather than randomised evidence.

page.mentor_intro: Infective endocarditis is a rare disease with outsized consequences, and its modern face has shifted: healthcare-associated infection, prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices, and staphylococci now dominate an epidemiology once ruled by viridans streptococci and rheumatic valves. The AHA scientific statement anchors diagnosis (modified Duke criteria), antimicrobial selection by organism and valve type, and complication management — heart failure, emboli, and the infected-device problems that need a team, not just a drug. Outcome still hinges on early recognition and the endocarditis-team model: infectious diseases, cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, and microbiology deciding together.

teaching_points.claim: Modern IE epidemiology is driven by healthcare exposure, prosthetic valves, and intracardiac devices, with Staphylococcus aureus now the leading organism in many series.

The AHA scientific statement standardises diagnosis (modified Duke criteria), antimicrobial therapy by organism and valve type, and management of complications including heart failure, embolism, and device infection.
Outcomes improve with a multidisciplinary endocarditis team; surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, and prevention of embolism in defined situations.
Blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography (TTE then TEE) are the non-negotiable first steps; the organism, not the syndrome, dictates the regimen.

uncertainties: Optimal duration and agent choice for device-related and culture-negative endocarditis remain guideline-extrapolated.
The role of routine PET/CT beyond prosthetic-valve and device infection is still being defined.

page.mentor_intro: Two numbers govern infective endocarditis treatment: the weeks of antibiotics and the timing of surgery. Duration is set by organism and valve — viridans streptococci on a native valve can be cured in two weeks with combination therapy, while staphylococci on prosthetic material demand six — and reviews of the ESC framework examine where shorter, equally effective courses can replace tradition. Surgery is lifesaving but high-risk: perioperative optimisation, the classic indications (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetations with embolic risk), and the modern operative challenges of extensive root destruction and device extraction define the contemporary craft.

teaching_points.claim: Antibiotic duration in IE is pathogen- and valve-specific: 2 weeks is possible for selected viridans-group streptococcal native-valve disease with suitable agents, while staphylococcal and prosthetic-valve infection typically requires 4-6 weeks.
Reviews of the ESC treatment framework examine strategies to treat more effectively — shorter total courses and early oral switch in stable, selected patients — without loss of cure rates.

Surgical indications remain heart failure from valvular dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent sepsis, prosthetic dehiscence), and embolism prevention for large/mobile vegetations, particularly with staphylococci.
Perioperative mortality in IE surgery is among the highest in cardiac surgery; preoperative optimisation of heart failure, sepsis, and organ dysfunction materially affects outcomes.

uncertainties: Whether further duration shortening (e.g. two weeks for staphylococcal native-valve IE with surgery) is safe is untested outside selected series.
Optimal timing of surgery after embolic stroke remains individualised by stroke severity and neuroimaging.

page.mentor_intro: The POET trial broke the oldest rule in endocarditis treatment: that cure demands six weeks of intravenous antibiotics. In stable, non-septic patients on effective IV therapy with susceptible organisms, switching to oral combination therapy was non-inferior — transforming an inpatient doctrine into an outpatient pathway. The modern literature formalises who qualifies: clinical stability, documented susceptibility, suitable oral-agent bioavailability, no uncontrolled foci or high-resistance organisms, and a reliable patient with follow-up. Not every endocarditis qualifies — but the default of 'IV until week six' is now a choice, not a law.

teaching_points.claim: Partial oral treatment (POET) is non-inferior to continued IV therapy in stable left-sided endocarditis caused by susceptible streptococci, enterococci, and S. aureus, after an initial effective IV period.
Eligibility for oral step-down demands clinical stability, organism susceptibility, high-bioavailability oral agents, absence of uncontrolled infection foci or abscess, and reliable follow-up.
Oral regimens typically use combination therapy (two agents with different mechanisms) to protect against resistance emergence given sub-therapeutic tissue levels risk.

Exclusions for oral switch include prosthetic-valve infection in the early post-operative period, uncontrolled sepsis, heart failure awaiting surgery, and organisms with reduced oral-susceptibility options.

uncertainties: Whether oral step-down applies to prosthetic-valve IE beyond selected low-risk cohorts is unresolved.
Optimal duration of the initial IV period before switching (2 versus 4 weeks) by organism remains centre-defined.

page.mentor_intro: The diagnostic spine of infective endocarditis is procedural discipline: at least three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before any antibiotics, followed by echocardiography — transthoracic first, transoesophageal when suspicion persists or prosthetic material is involved. The modified Duke criteria organise the result into definite, possible, and rejected, but their known weakness is sensitivity in the era of device infection and culture-negative disease, which is where advanced imaging earns its place. This topic is the instrument-focused view of the endocarditis cluster: get the cultures right, get the echo right, and the diagnosis usually declares itself.

teaching_points.claim: Blood-culture discipline: at least three sets from separate venepunctures over 12-24 hours before antibiotics, with cultures held for extended incubation when prior antibiotics were given.
Echocardiography follows a TTE-then-TEE logic: TEE is mandatory for prosthetic valves, persistent suspicion after negative TTE, and assessment of complications such as abscess and fistula.

The modified Duke criteria classify definite/possible/rejected endocarditis using major (positive echocardiogram, typical organism) and minor criteria; sensitivity limitations are increasingly recognised.

Surgical indications detected on imaging — heart failure from valve destruction, abscess/fistula formation, and persistent vegetations after emboli — convert the diagnostic pathway into an urgent surgical referral.

uncertainties: How to integrate PET/CT and cardiac CT into the Duke framework beyond prosthetic valves and devices is evolving.
Optimal echocardiographic vegetation-size threshold for surgery is informed by trial subgroup data rather than absolute rules.

page.mentor_intro: Empiric antibiotics in infective endocarditis are a narrowing problem: the 2015 AHA and ESC guidelines converge on organism-driven choices — antistaphylococcal cover for acute community or healthcare presentation, penicillin/ceftriaxone for subacute native-valve disease — while explicitly disagreeing in places that examiners probe. Two modern refinements: aminoglycoside synergism, long dogma for enterococcal and streptococcal IE, now carries documented nephrotoxicity without proven outcome benefit, and guidelines increasingly say goodbye; and enterococcal disease — increasingly ampicillin-resistant — forces regimen individualisation where bacteraemia and endocardia merge clinically.

teaching_points.claim: The 2015 AHA and ESC guidelines agree on organism-directed empiric therapy: cover S. aureus for acute presentations and healthcare-associated disease, and streptococcal cover with ceftriaxone/penicillin for subacute native-valve presentations pending cultures.
Empiric choices must anticipate the modern microbiology: staphylococci dominate healthcare-associated and device-related IE, with vancomycin reserved for MRSA risk or beta-lactam allergy.

Aminoglycoside synergy for enterococcal and streptococcal endocarditis is challenged by nephrotoxicity without demonstrated outcome benefit; contemporary analyses question their continued routine use.

Enterococcal bacteraemia and endocarditis management requires source assessment, susceptibility-guided regimens (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone for susceptible strains, daptomycin or linezolid for resistant), and infectious-disease input.

uncertainties: Whether combination beta-lactam therapy for MSSA bacteraemia/endocardia improves outcomes is unresolved.
The place of novel lipoglycopeptides (dalbavancin) and long-acting agents in outpatient IE pathways is under study.

page.mentor_intro: Inflammatory bowel disease — Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis — is managed at a genuinely modern pace: the 2025 British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines codify treat-to-target medicine with early biologic escalation, biomarker-guided monitoring, and an expanding small-molecule armamentarium. The core skill is no longer memorising drugs but running the disease: objective assessment (endoscopy, faecal calprotectin, CRP) rather than symptom guesswork, escalation before damage accumulates, and complication surveillance that changes with disease duration and extent. IBD is now a specialty where induction speed and monitoring discipline determine long-term outcomes.

teaching_points.claim: IBD management is treat-to-target: the BSG 2025 guidelines emphasise objective remission targets (mucosal healing, biomarker normalisation) with regular re-assessment rather than symptom-based adjustment.
Faecal calprotectin and CRP are the workhorse biomarkers for activity monitoring and relapse prediction, reducing but not replacing endoscopic assessment.

Therapy spans 5-ASA and steroids for UC, immunomodulators, biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab), and small molecules (JAK inhibitors, S1P modulators), selected by disease phenotype, severity, and prior response.

Complication surveillance — colorectal cancer screening by disease duration/extent in colitis, osteoporosis from repeated steroids, and vaccination before immunosuppression — is part of every IBD treatment plan.

uncertainties: Optimal first-line biologic selection (anti-TNF versus integrin versus IL-12/23) for individual phenotypes is partially answered by head-to-head data.
Whether biomarker-normalisation alone can substitute for scheduled endoscopy in sustained remission is being tested.

page.mentor_intro: Biologic therapy in IBD is a story of expanding options and sharpening precision. Five biologics are approved for ulcerative colitis with differing efficacy and positioning; after anti-TNF failure in Crohn's, indirect-comparison meta-analysis informs the vedolizumab-versus-ustekinumab choice that lacks a head-to-head trial; dual biologic therapy pushes the frontier for refractory disease at accepted infection-cost. And therapeutic drug monitoring has converted biologic prescribing from 'intensify and hope' to pharmacokinetic reasoning — low drug levels with antibodies point to switching class, low levels without antibodies to dose escalation. Modern IBD biologic care is applied pharmacology.

teaching_points.claim: Five biologics are approved for UC (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab) with differing efficacy and positioning; selection weighs disease severity, extraintestinal manifestations, and patient factors.

After anti-TNF failure in Crohn's disease, meta-analytic indirect comparison supports ustekinumab and vedolizumab as effective next-line options, with selection informed by phenotype and safety profile.

Dual biologic therapy (anti-TNF plus vedolizumab or ustekinumab) is an emerging strategy for refractory IBD with encouraging short-term outcomes in systematic review, at the cost of increased infection risk.

Therapeutic drug monitoring distinguishes mechanistic loss of response: low drug levels with anti-drug antibodies indicate switching class; low levels without antibodies indicate intensification — applying this prevents inappropriate escalation.

uncertainties: Whether dual biologics offer durable remission beyond small series, and their long-term safety, is unknown.
Optimal TDM thresholds and proactive-versus-reactive monitoring strategies are not fully standardised.

page.mentor_intro: The idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are a heterogenous family unified by proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase but divided by skin, lung, antibody, and histology — and the modern classification (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, anti-synthetase syndrome, inclusion body myositis) directly drives treatment. Dermatomyositis brings its cancer-surveillance duty and characteristic rashes; anti-synthetase syndrome brings the mechanic's-hands, fever, and interstitial lung disease that can dominate the prognosis; IBM (topic 925) resists immunotherapy by its degenerative core. First-line treatment remains high-dose corticosteroids with early steroid-sparing agents, with myositis-specific antibodies now guiding both prognosis and escalation choices.

teaching_points.claim: Modern classification divides IIM into dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, anti-synthetase syndrome, and inclusion body myositis — categories with distinct treatment responses and prognoses.
Dermatomyositis carries a malignancy association warranting age-appropriate cancer screening at diagnosis; characteristic cutaneous signs (heliotrope, Gottron papules) complement proximal weakness.

Anti-synthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1 and others) presents with myositis, mechanic's hands, fever, Raynaud, and interstitial lung disease; ILD severity often dictates the prognosis and escalation intensity.

First-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids with early addition of steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate, IVIG); myositis-specific antibodies increasingly inform prognosis and treatment selection.

uncertainties: Optimal steroid-sparing selection by myositis subtype and antibody profile is not standardised.
The role of rituximab and new targeted agents beyond refractory disease is still being defined.
